q: Does the Trotterised PITE algorithm extend cleanly to finite-temperature imaginary-time evolution (i.e., preparing thermal Gibbs states rho = exp(-beta H) / Z rather than only projecting onto the ground state), and if so how does the per-Trotter-step ancilla success probability scale with beta and system size when the target is a mixed state rather than a pure ground state?
basis: The paper focuses exclusively on zero-temperature ground-state preparation via large-beta projection from a fixed initial state. Its per-gadget success probability alpha^2 = exp(2|c_k| Delta tau) is derived under the assumption of applying exp(-c_k Delta tau sigma_k) to a pure state. Finite-temperature ITE typically requires purification (doubling the qubit register) or randomised state preparation with sampling over a thermal ensemble; neither is discussed and the scaling of cumulative post-selection cost under a mixed-state target is unknown.
next_steps: (1) Reimplement PITE on the doubled (system + purifier) register of a small 2-3 qubit toy Hamiltonian and initialise the purifier register in the maximally entangled state; run PITE only on system-side gadgets to arrive at rho(beta) after tracing out the purifier. (2) Compare against exact thermal state via numpy expm(-beta H). (3) Measure cumulative success probability as a function of beta at fixed spectral gap, and compare to the ground-state-projection scaling reported in the paper. (4) Test whether an adaptive-effort schedule (see Q5) helps or hurts thermal-state fidelity at fixed shot budget.

q: Can PITE be warm-started from a tensor-network (MPS or PEPS) approximation of the ground state so that the number of Trotter steps r --- and hence the cumulative success probability p ~ exp(-c r) --- is reduced by orders of magnitude for gapped 1D and quasi-1D lattice Hamiltonians?
basis: The paper's Fig 7 starts from the trivial |+>^{tensor n} product state and requires r=45 Trotter steps to reach |Delta E| ~ 2e-4 on 4-site TIM, with cumulative p_success ~ 6e-3. If the initial state already has ground-state overlap 1 - epsilon (rather than the ~4e-1 overlap of |+>^{tensor 4} with the TIM ground state at h=0.1), the required beta to reach the same energy error shrinks logarithmically in epsilon, and the exponential decay of p_success means orders-of-magnitude fewer shots. Tensor-network warm starts are cheap classically for gapped 1D but were not discussed.
next_steps: (1) On the same 4-site TIM at J=0.5, h=0.1, compute the MPS ground state at bond dimension chi in {2, 4, 8} via classical DMRG (quimb or itensor.jl). (2) Load the MPS into a qiskit Statevector as the PITE initial state (bond dimension 2 or 4 requires ~n log(chi) ancillas via Ran's construction). (3) Rerun PITE and measure the reduction in Trotter steps needed to reach |Delta E| = 2e-4 and the resulting cumulative p_success. (4) Repeat on 8- and 12-site TIM to see whether the warm-start advantage grows with system size, since standard PITE p_success is expected to collapse there.

q: How does the non-unitary Trotter PITE method perform on chemically relevant Hamiltonians (e.g., H2, LiH, H4 in a minimal basis under Jordan-Wigner) versus the standard variational-quantum-eigensolver (VQE) and against measurement-based QITE, in terms of (a) ground-state energy accuracy at fixed shot budget and (b) two-qubit gate count?
basis: The paper only tests spin (TIM) and simplified Hubbard Hamiltonians with small coefficient dynamic range. Real molecular Hamiltonians have many more Pauli terms (hundreds even for H2 in STO-3G under JW), large coefficient variation, and long CNOT ladders per Pauli gadget. The paper does not benchmark PITE against VQE, standard QITE (McArdle et al. 2019), or QITE variants (McClean-type projected QITE) on a common ground-state problem, so the practical advantage claim is unquantified for chemistry.
next_steps: (1) Use OpenFermion or qiskit-nature to build the H2/STO-3G qubit Hamiltonian at 0.74 A bond length (~15 Pauli terms after tapering). (2) Reimplement PITE, standard measurement-based QITE (McArdle 2019), and a UCCSD-VQE baseline within the same simulator. (3) At matched shot budget (e.g., 10^5, 10^6, 10^7 total ancilla measurements), plot |E - E_FCI| vs shot count for each method. (4) Repeat for LiH at 1.5 A and for H4 in a linear chain at 0.75 A spacing. (5) Report two-qubit gate count per Trotter step (PITE) or per variational step (VQE) so that the fair-cost tradeoff is explicit.

q: How robust is the non-unitary Trotter PITE step to realistic hardware noise --- in particular, mid-circuit measurement error on the ancilla, T1/T2 decoherence across the CNOT ladder plus Rx plus measurement plus reset sequence, and residual entanglement between the discarded ancilla and the system --- and does that noise convert cleanly into an effective decrease in per-Trotter-step p_success or does it actively corrupt the target state (biasing the converged energy)?
basis: All results in the paper (and in this replication) are ideal statevector. Mid-circuit measurement on superconducting hardware has typical fidelity 95-99% per shot, and PITE compounds one such measurement per Pauli term per Trotter step: a 45-step run on a 4-site TIM with (say) 10 Pauli terms is ~450 mid-circuit measurements per shot in a single run, which even at 99% fidelity is exp(-4.5) ~ 1% success on top of the algorithmic ~0.6% post-selection. Whether the failure mode is a benign p_success reduction (fine, just needs more shots) or a systematic bias in the converged energy (fatal to the algorithm) is not explored.
next_steps: (1) In qiskit-aer, run the ancilla-circuit form of PITE (already partially implemented in qiskit_full_ite.py) under a depolarising noise model calibrated to typical superconducting numbers (single-qubit err 1e-4, two-qubit err 1e-3, measurement err 1e-2). (2) Sweep noise strengths from 0 to 10x nominal and record both the converged |E - E_0| and the measured cumulative p_success. (3) Distinguish two failure modes: measurement error (biases the branch label) vs coherent gate error (biases the state within the accepted branch). (4) If a systematic bias emerges, test whether error-mitigation techniques (readout calibration, zero-noise extrapolation over the ancilla-only subcircuit) can suppress it back to the ideal curve.

q: Does an adaptive Trotter step-size schedule --- e.g., large Delta tau early (when the initial state is far from the ground state and the leading Trotter error is dominated by higher-lying eigenstates that PITE damps anyway) and small Delta tau near convergence (when the residual |Delta E| is dominated by Trotter error itself) --- reduce the total number of ancilla measurements needed to reach a target energy accuracy, and can the schedule be learned online from the observed per-step post-selection probability?
basis: The paper uses a single fixed Delta tau = 0.1 throughout all runs. Our data show that early Trotter steps see the energy drop by factors of 10 per unit beta, while late steps hit a plateau at |Delta E| ~ 2e-4 controlled by first-order Trotter error at Delta tau = 0.1; shrinking Delta tau by 10x late in the run would (naively) shrink the residual by 10x for free at the cost of only ~10x more steps, but no such schedule is explored. The p_success signal itself (observed drop per step) is a natural feedback signal for adapting Delta tau.
next_steps: (1) Extend ite_tim.py to accept a list of Delta tau values indexed by step. (2) Baseline: run at Delta tau = 0.1 for 45 steps (existing curve). (3) Schedule A: Delta tau = 0.2 for steps 0-9, Delta tau = 0.1 for 10-29, Delta tau = 0.05 for 30-89. Compare final |Delta E| and cumulative shot cost at matched integrated beta. (4) Schedule B: adapt Delta tau online by halving whenever the observed per-step |Delta E| reduction falls below a threshold. (5) On the harder 4-site Hubbard (paper's C6 regime), test whether the adaptive schedule buys enough headroom in p_success to reach it inside 10^7 shots instead of the paper's estimated 10^9.
